facts.title: Born in a Russian Lab
facts.text: Moscovium was first created in 2003 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in Dubna, Russia, by a Russian-American team led by Yuri Oganessian. Researchers fired a beam of calcium-48 ions at a target of americium-243, and the fusion of these nuclei produced a few atoms of element 115. The discovery was a collaboration between JINR and the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the United States.

facts.title: Named for Moscow Region
facts.text: The element was officially named Moscovium in 2016 by IUPAC, honoring the Moscow Oblast where Dubna and the JINR laboratory are located. Before that, it carried the placeholder name 'ununpentium' (literally 'one-one-five' in Latin) and the symbol Uup. The name follows a tradition of naming superheavy elements after the places or institutions that discovered them, just like dubnium, also named for Dubna.

facts.title: Vanishes in a Heartbeat
facts.text: Moscovium is extraordinarily unstable and radioactive, with even its longest-lived known isotope, moscovium-290, having a half-life of only about 0.65 seconds. Most isotopes decay in mere milliseconds by emitting alpha particles. Because of this fleeting existence, scientists have only ever made a handful of atoms at a time, never enough to see with the naked eye.

facts.title: A Stepping Stone to Other Elements
facts.text: When moscovium atoms undergo alpha decay, they transform into atoms of nihonium (element 113). In fact, the very experiments that confirmed moscovium also provided important evidence for nihonium's existence by observing the decay chains. This makes moscovium a kind of nuclear ancestor, helping researchers map out the behavior of several superheavy elements at once.

facts.title: Predicted to Be a Metal
facts.text: Moscovium sits in group 15 of the periodic table, directly below bismuth, so chemists expect it to behave as a heavy post-transition metal rather than like the nonmetals nitrogen and phosphorus higher in the column. Calculations suggest it could be a solid at room temperature with a density several times that of water. Because so few atoms exist for fractions of a second, almost everything we 'know' about its chemistry comes from theory, not laboratory measurement.

facts.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Atom
facts.text: In atoms as heavy as moscovium, the innermost electrons move at a substantial fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's theory of relativity strongly alters their behavior. These relativistic effects are predicted to change moscovium's expected chemistry, potentially making certain oxidation states more or less stable than simple periodic trends would suggest. Studying such effects is one of the main scientific reasons for creating superheavy elements at all.

facts.title: Edge of the 'Island of Stability'
facts.text: Moscovium lies near a long-theorized 'island of stability,' a region of the chart of nuclides where certain superheavy isotopes might survive far longer than their neighbors. Physicists hope that isotopes with just the right balance of protons and neutrons could last minutes, days, or even longer. Moscovium's measurable, sub-second half-lives are seen as encouraging hints that this island may really exist nearby.

facts.title: Made One Atom at a Time
facts.text: Creating moscovium is staggeringly inefficient: experimenters may run a particle accelerator for weeks, sending trillions upon trillions of calcium ions at the target, just to produce a single detectable atom. The successful fusions are identified not by seeing the element directly but by detecting the precise sequence and energy of alpha particles it emits as it decays. This detective-like analysis of decay chains is how its discovery was ultimately confirmed.

facts.title: Not Found in Nature
facts.text: Moscovium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth, in meteorites, or, as far as we know, in stars. It is entirely synthetic, existing only briefly inside specialized accelerator laboratories. Even the violent nuclear processes in supernovae are not thought to leave behind any lasting moscovium, because any that formed would decay almost instantly.

facts.title: No Uses Beyond Research
facts.text: Because it can only be made a few atoms at a time and disappears in under a second, moscovium has no commercial, industrial, medical, or biological role of any kind. Its entire value is scientific: it helps physicists test the limits of the periodic table and refine theories about how atomic nuclei hold together. Studying elements like moscovium deepens our fundamental understanding of matter, even though you will never find it in any product.
